newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - April 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - April 9.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Wednesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* Government antitrust regulators released new rules for evaluating mergers in light of cost savings and efficiencies.
* Motorola said the Securities and Exchange Commission was challenging its accounting treatment that let the company defer a $429 million gain on a sale of mobile radio properties in 1995.
* The Treasury's second auction of inflation-indexed bonds was not as successful as anticipated.
* The Dow Jones industrials finished at 6,609.16, up 53.25 points.
* Chrysler is expected to announce $1.2 billion investment plans for six Detroit plants, in order to boost light-truck and truck-engine production capacity.
* Designer Polo Ralph Lauren filed for a $600 million initial public offering.
* J.C. Penney's March same-store sales fell 3.7 percent. They were expected to be flat.
* Rather than wait for Congressional committee review, Rupert Murdoch is looking at whether his satellite-TV venture could move through Congress faster as part of a spending bill.
* Norfolk Southern and CSX announced the details of their plan to divide Conrail.
* Andy Grove, chief executive of Intel, got $94.6 million in 1996 by exercising stock options.
* Selling of large blocks of U.S.-listed stocks on foreign markets, also called "off-board" trades, is becoming popular.
* Seagate reported quarterly net income and sales figures which were ahead of analysts' expectations.
* H.F. Ahmanson reported a 59 percent increase in its quarterly profits.

* Heard on the Street: Some companies seem fated to pass from hand to hand like unwanted parcels, as successive owners try to squeeze money from the bundle of assets. Avis, the car-rental company now owned by HFS Inc, and United Press International are leading examples. So is Knoll, the maker of snazzy office furniture that still plans to come public despite the rocky market.
* Credit markets: Inflation-indexed notes, which got a lot of attention when they were introduced in January, aren't exactly selling like hot cakes. At least not yet.
